Art Nouveau was an international design movement spanning roughly 1890 to 1910 that revolutionized decorative arts, architecture, and graphic design by drawing inspiration from natural forms and rejecting industrial mass production. It celebrated sinuous plant forms, whiplash curves, and integrated ornament that reflected both aestheticist principles and anxieties about modernity. Though short-lived as a cohesive movement, Art Nouveau bridged the nineteenth-century Arts and Crafts tradition with twentieth-century modernism, leaving an indelible mark on furniture, jewelry, posters, and public spaces across Europe and America.

The movement flourished primarily between 1890 and 1910, with its peak popularity around 1900. It was named retrospectively and called Jugendstil in German-speaking countries and Modern Style in some English contexts. Art Nouveau rejected industrial mass production and machine aesthetics, embracing instead the handcrafted object as a rebellion against Victorian excess and mechanization—a position that paradoxically made Art Nouveau expensive and inaccessible to working classes. The aesthetic language drew from nature itself: flowing plant stems, insect wings, and organic curves rather than geometric or historical ornament, creating a visually distinctive vocabulary of sinuous lines and naturalistic motifs across all media.

The movement was exemplified by poster artist Alphonse Mucha, who created iconic theatrical advertising featuring androgynous figures with flowing hair and costumes integrated with floral frameworks that became the movement's visual signature. Landmark architectural and design works included Hector Guimard's Paris Metro station entrances, Louis Majorelle's furniture, Émile Gallé's glass vessels, and jeweler René Lalique's pieces that demonstrated Art Nouveau's reach across disciplines. The movement was particularly prevalent in Paris, Brussels, Vienna, and Barcelona, where local adaptations created regional variations. Art Nouveau declined after World War I, when modernism's geometric abstraction and industrial rationalism supplanted its craft-based organicism.
